title: Collapse adjacent equal group keys before HT probe in hash aggregate sink
hypothesis: In q18 the HASH_GROUP_BY in the IN-subquery (60M input rows, 15M groups, sum_no_overflow) takes 6.48s of CPU, about 75% of all operator time (wall time 0.85s). The input comes straight from a sequential scan whose rows are clustered on the group key: each key shows up as a run of roughly 4 adjacent rows. GroupedAggregateHashTable::AddChunk (src/execution/aggregate_hashtable.cpp:519) hashes every row and probes every row in FindOrCreateGroupsInternal. That means 60M random probes into a table of up to 1M entries, plus a row_matcher compare for each one, even though 3 of every 4 rows in a chunk have the same key as the row just before them. If we look up only the first row of each run and give that address to the rest of the run, hashing, probing and matching drop by about the average run length. UpdateAggregates/RowOperations::UpdateStates already handle duplicate addresses correctly, because the dictionary path (TryAddDictionaryGroups) relies on exactly that.
plan: In src/execution/aggregate_hashtable.cpp, add `optional_idx TryAddRunGroups(DataChunk &groups, DataChunk &payload, const unsafe_vector<idx_t> &filter)` and call it from AddChunk(groups, payload, filter) after TryAddCompressedGroups fails and before groups.Hash(). Guard: groups.size() >= 2, and every group column has a fixed-width physical type (no VARCHAR/BLOB, LIST, STRUCT or ARRAY; check TypeIsConstantSize on InternalType). Turn each group column into UnifiedVectorFormat. Walk i = 1..n-1 and mark row i as the start of a new run if any column differs from row i-1. Two rows count as equal only when both are NULL, or both are valid with identical bytes (memcmp of the value width). That is conservative: bytes that match are always the same group, and bytes that differ just fall through to the normal HT path. Bail out early (return invalid optional_idx and use the existing path) once the run-head count goes above n/2. Otherwise, the same way TryAddDictionaryGroups does it: build a SelectionVector of run heads, fill dict_state.unique_values (InitializeEmpty on first use) with Slice(groups, heads_sel, head_count), hash with dict_state.hashes, call FindOrCreateGroups(unique_values, hashes, dict_state.new_dictionary_pointers, state.new_groups), and keep the returned new-group count. If there are no aggregates, return now. Otherwise, for each row, set state.addresses[i] = head_ptr[run_of(i)] + layout_ptr->GetAggrOffset() (keep a running run index), then UpdateAggregates(payload, filter) and return the new-group count. sink_count is already incremented at the top of AddChunk. HLL only sees the head rows, which doesn't change the distinct estimate. This also covers the skip_lookups append path, which then appends one row per run.
expected_gain: q18: the subquery aggregate sink should get about 3-4x cheaper on hashing and probing. Expect -15 to -30% on q18 end-to-end. Finalize/combine cost doesn't change.
generality: Helps any GROUP BY whose input is clustered or sorted on the group keys: tables loaded in key order, time-series data grouped by timestamp or id, aggregates sitting above sort/merge-ordered or window outputs, and group-bys over a parent key in fact tables. For unclustered input the extra cost is one pass comparing adjacent rows, and it bails out as soon as more than half the rows start a run, so the worst case is a small regression on cheap high-cardinality aggregates with fixed-width keys.
risk: Low to medium. Correctness depends on duplicate addresses in UpdateStates, which the dictionary path already exercises. Have to make sure unique_values/dict_state isn't left in a state the dictionary path misreads (it resets by dictionary_id, and unique_values is re-sliced every time). Have to handle NULL validity properly. Distinct aggregates and filtered aggregates go through UpdateAggregates unchanged, so behaviour should be the same.

title: In-place finalize: combine radix partitions without re-materializing first-seen groups
hypothesis: The q18 subquery HASH_GROUP_BY (4.6-5.0s CPU, ~95% of the query) is bound by a fixed cost per group, not per input row. SQL experiments on the current build: orders GROUP BY o_orderkey (15M rows, 15M groups) takes 5.43s CPU, while lineitem GROUP BY l_orderkey (60M rows, 15M groups) takes 5.0s. 1.5M groups takes 0.48s, so ~320ns/group whatever the size, which means it is not about cache size. Removing the aggregate drops it to 3.17s and count(*) gives 4.29s, so the cost grows with row width. That points at row materialization and copying, not at probing (E0001 cut probes 4x and gained only ~1-3% wall). With 8 threads, every surviving group is materialized twice. Once in the sink (thread-local HT abandoned into partitioned TupleData). Then again in RadixHTLocalSourceState::Finalize, which calls ht->Combine(*partition.data): FlushMoveState scans and gathers the groups, FindOrCreateGroups appends a brand-new row (scatter plus InitializeStates) for every group first seen in the partition, then CombineStates. Later Scan gathers it again. For high-cardinality aggregates most groups are first-seen in finalize, so the second append, init and combine is pure copying. An in-place finalize would build only a pointer table over the existing partition rows. A first-seen row is used as the target directly, with no copy. A duplicate row gets its states combined into the target and is dropped. The scan then gathers from the list of live row pointers.
plan: 1) In src/execution/aggregate_hashtable.cpp (and its header), add GroupedAggregateHashTable::CombineInPlace(TupleDataCollection &data, vector<data_ptr_t> &live_rows). Scan `data` with TupleDataPinProperties::KEEP_EVERYTHING_PINNED, gathering the group columns and the hash as FlushMoveState does. Probe the ht_entry_t table using the same salt and linear-probing logic as FindOrCreateGroupsInternal. When a slot is empty, store the source row pointer itself with entry.SetPointer(source_row) and push it to live_rows; do not append. When the salt matches, compare with row_matcher.Match against the pointed-to rows. On a match, call RowOperations::CombineStates(source -> target). Simplest path: factor the probe loop so it returns an 'is new' selection plus target addresses without appending. 2) In src/execution/radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp, in RadixHTLocalSourceState::Finalize, use CombineInPlace only when !sink.external, !layout.HasDestructor() and sink.scan_pin_properties == DESTROY_AFTER_DONE (no multi-scan). Keep partition.data alive and pinned, and store live_rows in the AggregatePartition. Otherwise use the existing path. 3) In RadixHTLocalSourceState::Scan, when the partition has live_rows, take slices of up to STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE pointers into a row_locations Vector. Use data_collection.Gather(row_locations, sel, count, column_ids, scan_chunk, ...) for the group columns, then the existing FinalizeStates on those addresses. Reset the collection at the end. The HT pointer table can be freed right after finalize. Size the pointer table with GetCapacityForCount(partition.data->Count()), as is done today.
expected_gain: q18: the subquery aggregate drops one full row materialization (scatter, init, combine and the extra blocks) for ~all 15M groups. Estimate 15-25% of aggregate CPU, so roughly -10..-20% on q18 wall.
generality: Any multi-threaded hash aggregate with many groups, where groups mostly survive the thread-local HT uniquely: high-cardinality GROUP BY, DISTINCT, and the sub-aggregates in TPC-H q18/q10/q13-like shapes and in dedup queries. Low-cardinality aggregates have tiny partitions, so they see no change. Possible slowdowns: the scan gathers through random pointers instead of sequentially, so scan locality is a little worse. Pinning the whole partition while finalizing is the same as today's KEEP pin during combine.
risk: Medium. Correctness rests on (a) never destroying states of rows that are still live (restricted to layouts without destructors), (b) heap pointers for VARCHAR keys staying valid (KEEP_EVERYTHING_PINNED, non-external only), (c) multi-scan and external paths falling back. The bench verifies results on hidden shapes, so the fallback gates must be conservative.

title: Instrument and fix radix sink partition growth / repartition copies for high-cardinality aggregates
hypothesis: Group materialization costs ~320ns/group, and the cost grows with row width (no-agg 3.17s, count 4.29s, sum 5.43s CPU for 15M groups), which suggests repeated whole-row copies. RadixHTConfig::SetRadixBits is capped by ExternalRadixBits(true), which uses temporary_memory_state->GetReservation(). The initial reservation is only num_threads*ht_size, a few tens of MB, which may keep sink radix bits at InitialSinkRadixBits (3) or force repeated Repartition() copies of all thread-local data as bits grow by REPARTITION_RADIX_BITS, as MaybeRepartition shows. This is unverified: the first step is to log (debug only) final radix bits and the repartition count per thread on q18.
plan: First measure: temporary counters in MaybeRepartition (radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp) for repartition events and bytes moved. If repartitions move a large share of the data, start the sink at the maximum sink radix bits when the HLL/ADAPTIVITY decision shows high cardinality (in DecideAdaptation), so the data is partitioned once.
risk: Low-medium; memory-reservation interplay with external aggregation.

title: Skip unpartitioned staging for fixed-width group layouts in hash aggregate sink
hypothesis: Most of the q18 subquery aggregate cost is in the sink. I measured `SELECT l_orderkey, sum(l_quantity) FROM lineitem GROUP BY l_orderkey LIMIT 1` at about 410 ms. LIMIT 1 finalizes only a few partitions, and the full aggregate takes about 440 ms, so finalize is roughly 30-50 ms. A plain scan of lineitem is about 57 ms. The aggregate scales almost linearly with threads (4 threads 870 ms, 8 threads 455 ms, 16 threads 350 ms), so it is CPU-bound, not limited by memory bandwidth. Allocator flush settings had no effect. In FindOrCreateGroupsInternal (aggregate_hashtable.cpp:756-757), new groups go to `unpartitioned_data` when radix_bits >= UNPARTITIONED_RADIX_BITS_THRESHOLD (3) and new_entry_count/partitions <= 4. On q18 that is about 512 new groups per chunk over 128 partitions, which is exactly 4, so every group takes the staging path. Every Abandon(), which happens every ~16K groups because sink capacity is 32768, then does FlushAppendState, Unpin and Repartition into partitioned_data. Repartition uses DESTROY_AFTER_DONE, and its append state is new each time, so each abandon pins and unpins 128 partitions and frees and reallocates the staging blocks. So each of the 15M groups is written twice and copied once in the sink. An earlier run, recorded in the user's auto-memory, got about -5% on q16 by removing staging for heap layouts. For fixed-width rows, a single direct scatter into the partitions should be cheaper than scatter, copy and repartition.
plan: 1) Measure first. Add temporary steady_clock timers, removed before finishing, around the Repartition inside GroupedAggregateHashTable::Abandon (aggregate_hashtable.cpp:129-146) and around the AppendUnified call in FindOrCreateGroupsInternal (around :765). Report what share of sink time they take on `SELECT max(s) FROM (SELECT l_orderkey, sum(l_quantity) s FROM lineitem GROUP BY l_orderkey)`. 2) Change: in FindOrCreateGroupsInternal, take the unpartitioned path only when the layout is not all-constant, i.e. add `!layout_ptr->AllConstant()` to the condition at :756. Alternatively, lower the `<= 4` threshold for fixed-width layouts, e.g. to `< 2`; try both and keep the better one. Leave Abandon/AcquirePartitionedData unchanged: they already handle an empty unpartitioned_data. 3) Compare on and off with repeated `dbe-tool sql` runs (at least 5 warm runs each) of the isolated aggregate and of full q18, not only with bench against best.
expected_gain: q18 0-6% (the sink is about 60% of q18 wall time). The step 1 timers tell us whether the staging copy matters at all.
generality: High-cardinality GROUP BYs with fixed-width keys and states that run with many threads (>2) and reach 3+ radix bits: distinct-heavy group-bys, IN-subquery aggregates, and similar. Could get slower: aggregates with very few new groups per chunk spread over many partitions, where scattering into 128 partitions for a handful of rows has more per-partition overhead than the bulk repartition. Heap (VARCHAR) layouts are unchanged.
risk: Low. A one-condition change on a path that already exists (the partitioned path is used whenever new_entry_count/partitions > 4). Correctness is unaffected, because both paths feed the same partitioned_data.

title: Ablation-timed breakdown of radix agg sink per-group cost, then fix the top component
hypothesis: New R4 measurements (dbe-tool sql, hot, 8 threads): SELECT max(s) FROM (SELECT l_orderkey k, sum(l_quantity) s FROM lineitem GROUP BY k) = 455 ms (15M groups). The same with k = l_orderkey//64 (~230K groups, same 60M rows, same clustering) = 220 ms, and //4 (~3.75M groups) = 284 ms. A plain scan with the //64 expression = 115 ms. So the per-row agg path costs ~105 ms wall, and the per-GROUP cost is ~235 ms wall at 15M groups (~125 ns CPU/group, linear in group count). Single-threaded: //64 1.33 s vs full 5.18 s => ~257 ns/group. Three blind attempts at parts of this cost found nothing: E0001 probes (-13% CPU, ~0 wall), E0002 finalize re-materialization (0), E0003 unpartitioned staging (0). We are guessing component by component at 1 round each. One ablation round that times each sink sub-step on the 15M-group query will show which component holds the ~125 ns/group, and then allow a targeted fix in the same round.
plan: Step 1 (measurement, temporary code, never committed): in a scratch build, time the isolated query above (3+ hot runs each via dbe-tool sql; results may be wrong during ablation, which is fine because only timing matters) with each of these removed in turn: (a) RowOperations::InitializeStates in FindOrCreateGroupsInternal (aggregate_hashtable.cpp ~:766); (b) the UpdateAggregates call in GroupedAggregateHashTable::AddChunk (aggregate_hashtable.cpp ~:519 onward); (c) the Abandon()+MaybeRepartition block in RadixPartitionedHashTable::Sink (radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp :578-600), by forcing one big local HT instead (e.g. local_sink_capacity = 1<<22 after adaptation), which also tests 'fewer abandons'; (d) the hll.Update path (enable_hll), which only runs for the first 1M rows, as a sanity check; (e) the RadixHTLocalSourceState::Finalize/Scan work, by making GetData emit nothing once Finalize is done. Also compare with skip_lookups forced on (pure append, no probe) to separate probe from materialization. Record wall per variant in the ledger notes. Step 2 (real change): if (c) gives >=8%, implement a generality-safe capacity rule in DecideAdaptation (radix_partitioned_hashtable.cpp:424): when dedup is already near the HLL estimate (potential_increase_rate ~1) and the cardinality is high, grow local_sink_capacity up to an L2/L3-sized bound to cut abandon and repartition frequency. If (a) or (b) dominates, look for a per-call overhead fix in RowOperations::InitializeStates or AggregateExecutor scatter (e.g. a fast path for a single fixed-size state with a trivial initialize). If (e) dominates, revisit the source scan/finalize path. If nothing exceeds 8%, stop after step 1 and report the full table. Either result is useful.
expected_gain: q18: 0-15%. The measurement alone decides rounds 5-6. A step-2 fix that targets the dominant per-group component could reach 10-15% because the per-group cost is ~50% of the subquery aggregate.
generality: Every high-cardinality parallel hash aggregate (GROUP BY on a near-unique key, DISTINCT, IN/EXISTS subqueries with GROUP BY HAVING). A capacity-rule change could hurt low-dedup random-key aggregates if the HT outgrows cache, so bound it by L2/L3 size and gate it on the measured dedup ratio.
risk: Low for step 1 (temporary). Medium for step 2, depending on which fix. The memory interplay with external aggregation must be kept: never grow capacity when gstate.external.

title: Zonemap-prunable join key-set filter through compressed-materialization projections
hypothesis: After the 15M-group subquery agg, q18 rescans lineitem (60M rows: scan 0.16s + probe HASH_JOIN 0.26s CPU) and orders (15M rows: scan 0.20s + SEMI join 0.11s CPU) only to keep ~111 order keys. Both tables are stored clustered on the join key, so a key-set filter could skip most row groups through zonemaps. Two things currently block this. (1) JoinFilterPushdownOptimizer::GetPushdownFilterTargets / PushdownJoinFilterExpression (src/optimizer/join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp:23-56,144-160) stops at the `__internal_compress_integral_uinteger(#0, 1)` projection above each scan, because it accepts only BOUND_COLUMN_REF and integral BOUND_CAST. (2) JoinFilterPushdownInfo::CanUseInFilter (physical_hash_join.cpp:714) emits the zonemap-only IN filter only when ht->Count() <= dynamic_or_filter_threshold (default 50), and q18 builds about 111 keys. Measured with dbe-tool sql, full q18 LIMIT 1, alternating runs in one session with compressed_materialization disabled: threshold 50 gave 725 and 672 ms, threshold 1000 gave 604 and 574 ms (about -15%). EXPLAIN ANALYZE confirms 'optional: l_orderkey IN (...)' reaches the lineitem scan, and the lineitem probe join drops from 0.26s to 0.01s. With compression on, raising the threshold does nothing (590 vs 595), which confirms blocker (1). Disabling compression costs elsewhere, so the real fix must keep compression and push through it.
plan: Step A, push through compress: add `Value storage_offset` (null by default) to JoinFilterPushdownColumn (src/include/duckdb/execution/operator/join/join_filter_pushdown.hpp:25). In PushdownJoinFilterExpression, accept ExpressionClass::BOUND_FUNCTION when function.name starts with "__internal_compress_integral_", children[1] is a BoundConstantExpression, children[0] is integral and <= 64-bit, and no offset is set yet. Store the constant as storage_offset and recurse into children[0]. In JoinFilterPushdownInfo::FinalizeFilters and PushInFilter (physical_hash_join.cpp:720-911), when storage_offset is set, map each build-side compressed value v to the storage domain: cast v and the offset to HUGEINT, add them, then DefaultTryCastAs(storage_type), and skip the filter if that fails. Always skip the bloom filter when an offset is set (the has_cast check already does this; make it explicit). Validate step A with `SET dynamic_or_filter_threshold=1000` in dbe-tool sql: q18 should beat 595 ms. Step B, respect the threshold but still prune: when ht->Count() > threshold but <= a cap (e.g. 64*threshold, so ScanKeyColumn stays cheap), sort the unique non-null keys, keep the (threshold-1) largest gaps as boundaries, and push OptionalFilter(ConjunctionOrFilter of ConjunctionAndFilter(>=lo, <=hi)) with at most `threshold` ranges. ConjunctionOrFilter::CheckStatistics already prunes through zonemaps (conjunction_filter.cpp:10). Keep IsDenseRange/ContainsNull bail-outs. Do not change the setting default (rules.md forbids it).
expected_gain: q18 -5..-12%: about 0.45s CPU on lineitem scan+probe and about 0.3s on orders scan+semi, of which most row groups become prunable.
generality: Any selective hash join whose probe side is a scan clustered or sorted on the key (date and id joins, IN-subqueries over fact tables, star joins with filtered dimensions), now also through the compress projections that compressed materialization inserts on most large joins. Possible slowdowns: building and sorting up to a few thousand keys per join finalize, plus per-row-group checks of up to 50 ranges. Both are tiny, and the filter is optional (zonemap only), so it does no row-level work.
risk: Medium-low. Correctness depends on the offset mapping (overflow is handled through HUGEINT and the try-cast bail-out), and the filter is optional, so a wrong prune is the only failure mode. Range bounds must be inclusive and computed in the storage type. NULL keys: keep the existing ContainsNull bail-out.

title: Extra selectivity for HAVING-style aggregate-result range filters in join ordering
hypothesis: In q18 the customer HASH_JOIN costs 0.39s CPU plus 0.12s for the customer scan, about 55 ms of wall time. Measured: full q18 is about 577 ms, the variant without customer about 522 ms, the aggregate alone about 470 ms. That join builds a 1.5M-row hash table (keys span 1.5M values, above PerfectHashJoinExecutor MAX_BUILD_SIZE=1048576, so no perfect HJ) and is probed by only 111 rows. Customer is chosen as the build side because the SEMI-joined orders side is estimated at ~3.5M rows. The IN-subquery is Projection->Filter(sum(x) > c)->Aggregate(~14M groups), and the HAVING filter gets only the generic DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY 0.2 (relation_manager.cpp:274-277, aggregate case in ExtractJoinRelations). A hand-written variant that caps that side (LIMIT 100000, results identical) makes the optimizer build on the small side and probe customer. Alternating runs: 511/551 ms vs 551/574 ms for the original, about -5%. Filters on group keys are normally pushed below the aggregate, so the filters that stay above it are mostly range predicates on aggregate results (heavy-hitter or tail filters such as sum > c or count >= c). These usually keep a small fraction of the groups, so 0.2 is too generous.
plan: In src/optimizer/join_order/relation_manager.cpp, ExtractJoinRelations, case LOGICAL_AGGREGATE_AND_GROUP_BY (around line 265): after ExtractAggregationStats and the existing `if (!datasource_filters.empty())` multiplication by DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY, add a static helper `FilterHasAggregateRangePredicate(datasource_filters, aggr.aggregate_index)`. It walks each LogicalFilter's expressions and their AND conjunctions. It returns true if some conjunct is a BoundComparisonExpression of type GREATERTHAN/GREATERTHANOREQUALTO/LESSTHAN/LESSTHANOREQUALTO where one side is a BoundColumnRefExpression with binding.table_index == aggr.aggregate_index and the other side IsFoldable(). If it returns true, multiply operator_stats.cardinality by DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY once more (at most once in total), clamped to >= 1. Do NOT change aggr.SetEstimatedCardinality (the aggregate's own estimate stays). Use LossyNumericCast like the surrounding code. Verify with EXPLAIN on q18 that customer becomes the probe side of its join (the ~111-row side should build) and that the lineitem join still builds on the small side. Then bench q18. If the flip does not happen, print the semi-RHS estimate and check that the filter really is in datasource_filters for this aggregate (the RHS goes through LOGICAL_PROJECTION -> AddRelationWithChildren -> child optimizer). If needed, also consider the equivalent path at line 198. No setting or default changes.
expected_gain: q18: -5..-8% (customer build of ~0.4s CPU replaced by probing 1.5M rows against a ~111-row table)
generality: Any query that joins an IN/EXISTS subquery or derived table with a HAVING range predicate on an aggregate (top spenders, groups with count > N, large orders) to other tables. The smaller estimate lets the join order put that side on the build side and probe the big dimension. Queries whose HAVING keeps most groups could get a worse join order: they would build on a side that is larger than estimated. Results stay correct because only estimates change.
risk: Low for correctness (only cardinality estimates change). Medium for plan regressions on hidden queries with non-selective HAVING clauses. Also check that the expression walk handles nested conjunctions and casts on the column side (it can simply not match).

title: Allow more zonemap ranges than dynamic_or_filter_threshold in key-range join filter
hypothesis: E0005 pushes at most 50 merged ranges for about 111 keys. The lineitem probe scan still emits 17.5M of 60M rows, while with one key per row group about 13.6M would be the floor. Checking a row group against a range set is cheap, so a separate cap (for example 1024 ranges, binary search over sorted ranges) would prune more.
plan: physical_hash_join.cpp range-set path from E0005: use its own constexpr cap on the number of ranges instead of dynamic_or_filter_threshold. Possibly also replace the OR-of-ranges filter with a sorted-range filter that checks statistics by binary search.
generality: Hash joins with a small, scattered build key set over clustered probe tables.
risk: Low; the gain is probably below noise.
